source: Wilhelm et al. (2011) Sleep selectively enhances memory expected to be of future relevance
finding: Exp 1: word pairs learned, then subjects were told (or not) that recall would be tested after 9 h. Telling them only helped after sleep, not after wake. Telling was done AFTER learning, so encoding depth was the same.
numbers: 142 adults tested. Final n: sleep expected 18, sleep unexpected 28, day-wake 15 vs 32, night-wake 19 vs 30. Retention (criterion trial = 100%): sleep expected 117.29+-3.54, sleep unexpected 105.23+-3.01 (p=0.014); expectancy x sleep/wake interaction p=0.05. Wake groups 96.7 to 104.9, no expectancy effect (p>0.49). Unexpected-sleep not different from wake (p>0.25).
quote: Sleep to a greater extent consolidates memories that are expected to be recalled later
limits: Interaction only p=0.05. Subjects who suspected the test were dropped (n=10, 17, 11) and looked like the expected group. Lab sample of young students, short-term word lists.
agent_relevance: The same lesson is kept or lost depending on a later-use signal set AFTER it was stored. A memory store can gate keeping on an expected-use flag, not on encoding quality.

source: Wilhelm et al. (2011) Sleep selectively enhances memory expected to be of future relevance (Exp 2, other task types)
finding: Exp 2 extended the effect to a nonverbal declarative task (card locations) and a procedural task (finger tapping). Expectancy raised overnight retention in both.
numbers: 49 adults (expected n=21, unexpected n=27 of whom 10 excluded). Card locations: 98.80+-4.92% vs 73.13+-9.08% (p=0.019). Finger tapping gain: 131.13+-4.08% vs 116.95+-5.04% (p=0.037). Novel sequence after test: no group difference (p>0.93), so effect is specific to the learned item.
limits: Small groups. No wake control in Exp 2, so sleep-specificity rests on Exp 1.
agent_relevance: Relevance gating is not limited to facts; it also applies to skills. A skill/procedure lesson can be prioritised by expected reuse.

source: Wilhelm et al. (2011) Sleep selectively enhances memory expected to be of future relevance (controls and sleep physiology)
finding: Expectancy did not act through rehearsal or retrieval priming. A surprise second recall 30 min later kept the gap. Expected subjects had more deep sleep and more slow oscillation power, and these predicted retention only in the expected group.
numbers: Stage 4 sleep: 8.2+-1.43% vs 4.07+-1.16% (p=0.03) in Exp 1; 11.72 vs 5.11% (p=0.01) in Exp 2. Slow oscillation power in first 20 min NREM vs retention r=0.71 (p<0.01) expected group, r=-0.25 unexpected. Second surprise recall still better in expected group (p=0.03).
quote: expectancy-induced improvement in overnight retention was not abolished when retrieval came as a surprise
limits: Correlations with small n (18 per group). Spindle count difference not significant in Exp 1 (316 vs 198, p=0.15).
agent_relevance: The relevance tag works through reactivation during offline time, not through the later test. For an agent: do the consolidation step AFTER the tag arrives, and prefer an offline pass over inline rehearsal.

source: Feld and Born (2020; online 2019) Neurochemical mechanisms for memory processing during sleep
finding: States the reconciliation: active systems consolidation (strengthen) and synaptic homeostasis (erase weak traces) look contradictory, but the fate of a trace may depend on its relevance for the future. Relevant memories are strengthened and irrelevant ones may be erased.
numbers: Cites Wilhelm 2011 as the instruction example; rewards and emotions also modulate sleep benefit. No new data on the relevance idea itself.
quote: the fate of a memory trace may be mediated by its relevance for the future
limits: It is a proposal in a review, stated as 'may', and the authors say what sets the direction of plasticity is still unclear.
agent_relevance: This is the design principle for the lesson store: one pass, two outcomes. Strengthen what is likely to be used, drop what is not.

source: Feld and Born (2020; online 2019) Neurochemical mechanisms for memory processing during sleep (dopamine and reward tag)
finding: Two accounts for how reward selects memories for sleep: (1) hippocampal replay drives striatum/VTA dopamine during sleep; (2) a dopamine tag is set at learning and sleep replay then runs without more dopamine. Human drug data favour the tag account.
numbers: Pramipexole (D2 agonist) before sleep wiped out the high-over-low reward advantage in recognition but left the encoding-duration benefit. Sulpiride (D2 blocker, ~60% receptor block) did not change the reward advantage (bioRxiv follow-up, cited).
limits: Reviewed, not opened at primary level. D1 receptors not excluded. Mixed dopamine drug results.
agent_relevance: Supports a two-step design: tag value when the lesson is written, then let a later job act on the tag. No need for a live value signal at consolidation time.

source: Feld and Born (2020; online 2019) Neurochemical mechanisms for memory processing during sleep (strength is not relevance)
finding: The relevance effect is not just memory strength: weak traces are replayed more during rest and gain more from sleep, so relevance picks different items than strength does.
numbers: Cites work showing weaker encoded memories are more likely replayed and benefit more from sleep. No numbers given in the review.
limits: Review claim; underlying studies not read here.
agent_relevance: Do not rank lessons by how well they were learned or how confident the agent was. Rank by expected use. These can point in opposite directions.

source: Feld and Born (2020; online 2019) Neurochemical mechanisms for memory processing during sleep (SHY and ASC compared)
finding: Synaptic homeostasis says sleep downscales weak synapses and spares strong ones. Active systems consolidation says replay moves hippocampal traces to cortex. Sharp-wave ripples are linked to both strengthening and hippocampal downscaling.
numbers: Notes human evidence for homeostasis mainly comes from better new learning after sleep. Timing of reactivation in hippocampal sub-regions during ripples may decide potentiation vs depression.
limits: The review says direct evidence linking selective downscaling to better memory is still missing.
agent_relevance: Two jobs in one pass: promote and prune. Pruning also frees room for new lessons.

source: Saletin, Goldstein and Walker (2011) The role of sleep in directed forgetting and remembering of human memories
finding: Words were cued Remember or Forget before a nap or no nap. Sleep boosted recall of Remember words but did not boost Forget words. So sleep honours a cue given while awake.
numbers: 46 adults (nap n=23, no-nap n=23). Group x cue-type interaction F(2,43)=6.17, p=0.004. Main group effect F(1,44)=6.44, p=0.015. R-F efficiency larger in nap group t(44)=2.18, p=0.03. Immediate memory equal across groups.
quote: sleep, relative to time awake, can selectively ignore the facilitation of items previously cued to be forgotten
limits: Free recall after a nap, small n. Forget words were not harmed (no drop vs wake), only not helped.
agent_relevance: 'Forget' is not an active delete here; it is non-promotion. A lesson tagged as irrelevant just stops getting boosts and fades.

source: Saletin, Goldstein and Walker (2011) The role of sleep in directed forgetting and remembering of human memories (spindle link)
finding: The remember-minus-forget advantage tracked fast sleep spindles over left superior parietal cortex (P3).
numbers: Pearson r=0.66, p=0.0006 after correction for multiple comparisons. Slow spindles showed no such link.
limits: Correlation in a nap group of 23. Source analysis is indirect.
agent_relevance: Selectivity needs a specific mechanism, not general sleep. The agent's prune/promote step should be a distinct operation with its own trigger.

source: Oudiette, Antony, Creery and Paller (2013) The role of memory reactivation during wakefulness and sleep in determining which memories endure
finding: Value-tagged object locations: low-value items lost more over a 90 min nap or wake. Replaying sounds of half the low-value items during slow-wave sleep rescued ALL low-value items, so reactivation, not value itself, decides what endures.
numbers: 60 young adults, 4 experiments (n=15 each). Pre-nap recall: 30.5 vs 23.6 items for high vs low value (F(1,56)=60.6). Exp I loss for low minus high value 1.05+-0.15 cm error, F(1,14)=11.6, p=0.004. Exp II with sound cues: 0.30+-0.09 cm, p=0.2; cue x experiment F(1,28)=5.0, p=0.03.
quote: covert reactivation is a major factor determining the selectivity of memory consolidation
limits: Only 90 min. Cue worked on whole low-value category in sleep (not item specific). Wake cueing helped only cued items. REM duration correlated with loss, speculative.
agent_relevance: A value tag changes how often an item is replayed. Replay frequency is the lever: a scheduler that raises replay for a low-priority lesson can save it. Keep/drop is a reactivation policy.

source: Oudiette, Antony, Creery and Paller (2013) The role of memory reactivation during wakefulness and sleep in determining which memories endure (REM and forgetting)
finding: Authors suggest REM may actively weaken low-value memories after slow-wave replay, and that cueing in SWS stabilises items otherwise erased in later REM. This follows Crick and Mitchison 1983.
numbers: Exp I decline in memory for low-value items correlated with REM duration (reported in text; exact r not extracted here).
limits: Speculation by authors; exact values not captured. Conflicts with Diekelmann and Born 2010 who give REM a strengthening role.
agent_relevance: Two phases may be useful: replay-strengthen first, prune second. Pruning should come after the promotion pass has had a chance.

source: van Dongen et al. (2012) Sleep supports selective retention of associative memories based on relevance for future utilization
finding: Within-subject version: two picture-location sets, told afterwards that only one would be retested. Sleep kept the relevant set better; daytime wake lost the relevant set MORE than the irrelevant one.
numbers: 50 analysed (10 excluded for doubting the instruction). 3-way interaction F=13.19, p=0.001. Sleep: relevant minus irrelevant retention = 1.3+-0.6 (p=0.045); wake: -1.7+-0.6 (p=0.005). Sleep vs wake on relevant items: 3.2+-1.0 (p=0.003); irrelevant: 0.2+-0.9 (p=0.83). Time asleep correlated with retention of relevant only.
limits: Baseline group difference on irrelevant items (SLEEP better, p=0.04); excluding 2 poor wake subjects removed it and effects held. 14 h delay, 60-item sets.
agent_relevance: Supports replication of Wilhelm in a different task. The wake reversal suggests that a relevance flag without an offline pass can backfire.

source: Barner, Werner, Schoerk, Born and Diekelmann (2023) The effects of sleep and targeted memory reactivation on the consolidation of relevant and irrelevant information (Exp 1)
finding: Weaker replication: picture-location sets, one declared relevant after learning. Relevant set kept better overall and sleep helped, but the sleep x relevance interaction was NOT significant. Planned contrasts showed a sleep advantage only for relevant items, growing at 1 week.
numbers: n=28 sleep, 28 wake. Sleep effect F(1,54)=6.71, p=0.012; relevance effect F(1,54)=8.78, p=0.005. Interaction p=0.12 overall, p=0.35 at 12 h, p=0.096 at 1 week. Sleep group relevant vs irrelevant at 1 week t(27)=2.75, p=0.01; wake t(27)=0.47, p=0.64. Retention at 12 h: sleep relevant 58.7 vs irrelevant 44.5; wake 41.1 vs 34.5.
quote: tentative evidence that the selective benefit of sleep for relevant memories evolves over time
limits: Key interaction failed. Authors call the evidence tentative. Participants needed more trials to learn the relevant set (p=0.039), a possible confound.
agent_relevance: The relevance x sleep effect is small and fragile. Plan for a modest gain from relevance-gated keeping, and test it.

source: Barner, Werner, Schoerk, Born and Diekelmann (2023) The effects of sleep and targeted memory reactivation on the consolidation of relevant and irrelevant information (Exp 2, TMR)
finding: Odor cueing during slow-wave sleep did not preferentially help relevant memories. Authors confirm relevant > irrelevant but cueing added nothing selective.
numbers: Odor n=23, vehicle n=20 (Exp 2). Main effect of relevance replicated; TMR x relevance not significant at the first SWS or after 1 week.
limits: Odor cue only; sound or item-specific cueing may differ. Small groups.
agent_relevance: Pushing replay at items did not amplify the relevance advantage. Do not assume more rehearsal of a flagged lesson helps more.

source: Barner, Werner, Schoerk, Born and Diekelmann (2023) The effects of sleep and targeted memory reactivation on the consolidation of relevant and irrelevant information (list of failures in intro)
finding: The intro lists support for relevance effects (expectancy, reward, emotion, intentions) and also failures: Brokaw 2016, Wamsley 2016, Barner 2018, Lipinska 2019, Schaefer 2020 found weak or no preferential consolidation.
numbers: Strongest support is cited from expectancy and reward manipulations (Fischer and Born 2009, Wilhelm 2011, van Dongen 2012).
limits: Citation list only; the failed studies were not read.
agent_relevance: Sets the base rate: the field is split. Treat relevance-based keeping as a hypothesis to test, not a law.

source: Davidson, Joensson, Carlsson and Pace-Schott (2021) Does sleep selectively strengthen certain memories over others based on emotion and perceived future relevance?
finding: Systematic review. Majority of studies do not support that sleep selectively favours emotional or future-relevant memories. Reward is best supported: sleep x reward interaction in about half of studies.
numbers: Test-expectancy: 3 studies found a sleep benefit when a retest is expected (one lacked a wake control), 2 found none, 1 found the opposite with post hoc subjective expectancy. Wamsley 2016 (n=75 and 94, maze and motor task): no interaction for either task. Subjective relevance: only one study clearly positive. Forgetting instructions: scattered and inconsistent. No sleep variable reliably tied to selection.
quote: the majority of studies does not support such an effect
limits: Narrative review, no effect-size pooling. Searched peer-reviewed human studies.
agent_relevance: A fair counterweight to Feld and Born. The relevance idea is plausible but roughly half-supported. Build the agent step as a testable switch with a plain no-gating arm.

source: Kurdziel et al. (2025) Top-down instruction outweighs emotional salience
finding: Directed-forgetting words (neutral and negative) over 12 h of sleep or wake. Instruction to remember beat emotion, but sleep did not change behavioural memory, so no sleep-selective effect in behaviour.
numbers: Two studies: online (Study 1) and in-lab with EEG (Study 2). Remember instruction raised recognition and recall; emotion gave no consistent benefit; sleep condition had no effect on performance. Spindle activity predicted recall of negative remember-cued words; SWS and delta power correlated negatively with total recall.
quote: sleep condition did not impact memory performance
limits: Sample sizes not extracted here. Behavioural null on sleep. EEG links are correlational.
agent_relevance: Another case where an explicit instruction mattered more than the offline step. The cue itself carries the value.

source: Theta oscillations tag episodic memories for sleep-dependent consolidation (PLOS Biology, 2026)
finding: EEG at learning can tell apart items later kept after sleep from items kept after wake. Theta (3-8 Hz) at learning for sleep-kept items predicted slow oscillation-spindle coupling in the nap, which predicted better recall. First human evidence for a tag set at learning.
numbers: 31 adults, within-subject 2 h nap vs wake. Retention better after sleep t(30)=2.49, p=.019, d=0.45. Associative memory change: -12.33 (sleep) vs -19.88 (wake). Classifier cluster at 0.87-1.13 s, p=.010, d=0.72; immediate-test classifier not significant (p=0.08).
limits: Short nap, young students, word-object pairs. Theta tag not shown to carry relevance, only sleep-bound fate.
agent_relevance: Backs the tag-at-write design. The decision to consolidate is made when the lesson is written, from a signal available then.

source: Fischer and Born (2009) Anticipated reward enhances offline learning during sleep
finding: Motor skill: two finger sequences trained; a monetary reward was announced after training for one. Sleep gain was larger for the rewarded sequence. After wake, little or no gain.
numbers: Abstract only: sleep gain greater for rewarded sequence regardless of training order; 12 h nocturnal sleep vs daytime wake.
limits: Abstract read, full paper not opened. Effect sizes not captured.
agent_relevance: Earliest reward-based sleep selectivity result; cited by Wilhelm 2011 and Barner 2023 as the strongest evidence.

source: Stickgold and Walker (2013) Sleep-dependent memory triage: evolving generalization through selective processing
finding: Proposes a two-step memory triage model: first pick which memories go through sleep processing, then choose the processing form (stabilise, integrate, abstract). Selection can be guided by emotion, reward, and cue instructions given around encoding.
numbers: Reports that in Wilhelm 2011 SWA and spindle correlations with retention were seen only in the group told to expect a test.
quote: sleep is ecologically guided by qualitative features evoked or presented in the peri-encoding period
limits: Perspective piece. Model not formal; no parameters.
agent_relevance: A direct template: triage then process. Gives a two-stage consolidation job with different outputs per lesson.

source: Rouast and Schoenauer (2023) Continuously changing memories: a framework for proactive and non-linear consolidation
finding: Argues memories stay malleable and are shaped repeatedly according to anticipated demand, in a flexible and reversible way, not a one-way move to cortex.
numbers: Abstract only. No numbers.
limits: Abstract read, full text not opened. Framework, not tested model.
agent_relevance: Keep/drop should be revisable. A lesson dropped today may need to return if its expected use changes.

source: Lewis and Durrant (2011) Overlapping memory replay during sleep builds cognitive schemata
finding: Mechanism model: related memories replay in overlapping combinations, so shared elements are strengthened and schemas build up.
numbers: Abstract only. No quantitative data.
limits: Abstract read only. Linked to subfield 09 (gist extraction).
agent_relevance: Relevance can be computed as overlap with other lessons: shared structure survives, one-off detail fades. See sibling subfield on gist.

source: Tononi and Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (SHY)
finding: Synaptic homeostasis: sleep renormalises net synaptic strength by down-selecting synapses, which also helps memory acquisition, consolidation and integration. This is the erase half of the Feld and Born reconciliation.
numbers: Abstract only. No numbers.
limits: Abstract read only. Feld and Born say selective downscaling for memory is not yet directly shown.
agent_relevance: Gives a theory for pruning: global downscale plus protect what replay engaged. A decay-all, refresh-used rule for the lesson store.

source: Diekelmann and Born (2010) The memory function of sleep
finding: Active systems consolidation: during slow-wave sleep, slow oscillations, spindles and ripples coordinate reactivation and redistribution of hippocampal memories to cortex. REM supports synaptic consolidation.
numbers: Abstract only. Used as the base account by Wilhelm 2011 and Barner 2023.
limits: Abstract read only. Review, not new data.
agent_relevance: The consolidation account to which relevance adds a selection rule.

source: Brokaw et al. (2016) Resting state EEG correlates of memory consolidation
finding: Not a relevance study but listed as a failure to find relevance effects by Barner 2023 (cited as such). It showed 15 min of quiet rest improved story recall with slow oscillation and low alpha.
numbers: n=26; eyes-closed rest vs distractor task for 15 min. Rest improved recall. Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only. Its role in the relevance debate is as cited by Barner 2023, not verified here.
agent_relevance: Consolidation may happen during any quiet period, so an agent can run keep/drop in idle time, not only after a task.

source: Antony and Schechtman (2023) Reap while you sleep: consolidation of memories differs by how they were sown
finding: Review of targeted reactivation in complex memory networks: outcomes depend on how memories interact when learned. Some interact helpfully, some antagonistically and impair retrieval.
numbers: Review; no pooled numbers extracted.
limits: Review only. Relevance is not the focus.
agent_relevance: The result of reactivating a lesson depends on the other lessons it was learned beside. Keep/drop should look at related lessons, not one in isolation.
